transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-02-17 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Connor (Redwood SE), Alex (Crestline CTO), Priya (ML Lead), Jordan (Infra)

Summary / Notes (auto):
Customer uses a mix of chat and classification models, peak token rate estimated at 12M tokens/day with spiky diurnal patterns. Priority: predictable latency (95p < 220ms for short chat) and strict tenant isolation for regulated customers. Wants both guaranteed baseline throughput and burst guardrails.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intros, i'm maya from redwood and connor is our se, alex do you want to kick off with a quick context?
[00:16] Alex: sure, yeah thanks maya. so crestline builds a document ingestion + summarization layer used by a set of regulated clients, we're exploring replacing our homegrown serving layer with either hosted or dedicated from you folks, main driver is predictability and compliance.
[00:34] Priya: and from ML we care about latency and prompt fidelity, so we want to avoid big quality diffs when you apply quant or batching.
[00:45] Connor: got it. when you say predictability, are you thinking about reserved GPUs / committed pool or more of a hybrid warm-pool with burst on demand?
[00:55] Alex: reserved pools plus burst protection. baseline traffic is steady-ish but every morning we get a spike where throughput increases ~3x for 20-40 minutes, and then there are ad-hoc bursts. so we need pre-warm or instant capacity to keep 95p latency tight.
[01:12] Jordan: security side we're under SOC two and need KMS integration, audit logs, and V P C peering. ideally we want customer-managed keys, hsm, the usual.
[01:25] Maya: that's good context. quick plug — Redwood Dedicated offers reserved GPU pools with autoscale policies and warm pools for pre-warm. we do offer customer KMS, audit logs, and VPC options in Private — and for Dedicated we can do V P C peering plus KMS integrations.
[01:44] Priya: can you explain how warm pools work vs prefix KV cache? sometimes in other systems the cache invalidates and you see cold starts.
[01:56] Connor: yeah so warm pools are about pre-allocated instances with model loaded and kv cache warm for common prefixes, while prefix K V cache sits in memory to skip re-exec for repeated prompts. still you'll see degradation on completely novel prompts, but for our bots the warm path reduces first-token latency a lot.
[02:20] Alex: what about contention across tenants? we need strict isolation for specific clients, not just soft quotas.
[02:29] Maya: we can offer isolated node groups (tenant fencing) so certain tenants run on dedicated nodes, and other tenants share the residual pool. that comes with a capacity commitment premium.
[02:40] Jordan: for the isolated nodes, do we get physical or logical isolation? we run other sensitive workloads so physical-ish segregation is preferred.
[02:49] Connor: we support allocation on dedicated GPU hosts per tenant when you need it; it's not multi-tenant on the same GPU. it's essentially node-level isolation. there are options for network segmentation too.
[03:02] Priya: how do you handle model variants? we train both a full fp16 model and a quantized variant; routing needs to prefer full model for priority users but fallback to quantized when capacity constrained.
[03:15] Connor: you can route by policy — latency-first routes to the full model on reserved capacity, cost-first routes to quantized on lower tiers. we also support automatic fallback so requests are retried against the fallback model if the primary is full or times out.
[03:30] Alex: curious about our SLOs — we want 95th < 220ms for short chat (~64 tokens) and 99th < 500ms. are those realistic on Dedicated?
[03:43] Connor: yes for the most part on dedicated reserved capacity with warm pools and proper batching config. actual numbers vary by model and sequence length. we typically run benchmarks for the customer workload — will need your token distribution to estimate.
[03:58] Maya: action item — we'll ask for the sample token distribution and top prompts. that helps sizing.
[04:06] Priya: we'll export a week's worth of inference logs, should show the spikes.
[04:12] Alex: another area is failover — if the reserved pool hits capacity or a region has issues, we need an automatic fallback (either to hosted or to a lower tier) without user-visible errors. how does redwood do that?
[04:26] Connor: we have smart routing and regional fallback, you can define policies: fail open to hosted variants or degrade to quantized model in same pool. there is also canary and A B rollout support so you can test fallback behavior first.
[04:40] Jordan: are you able to simulate network partitions in the POC? we want to see how a V P C peer failure would affect routing.
[04:50] Connor: yes we can include network partition scenarios in the POC script. we also capture traces and span-level logs so you can see where latencies spike.
[05:02] Alex: any constraints on sequence length? some of our summarization jobs go north of 4k tokens.
[05:09] Connor: sequence length affects memory and kernel selection; very long sequences will need larger GPUs or sharded execution. for 4k we typically recommend model variants optimized for longer context and perhaps partitioned KV cache. we'll include recommendations in the sizing doc.
[05:27] Priya: what's the typical cold-start for a quantized vs fp16 model? we've seen minutes on other platforms which is problematic.
[05:36] Connor: with warm pools and kept-KV it should be sub-second to first token for hot prefixes; cold-start to load model can be on the order of 10-40s depending on size unless kept resident. that's why reserved capacity helps. quantized models sometimes load faster but it's not guaranteed.
[05:54] Maya: pricing question — Alex, are you more sensitive to unit cost or to predictable monthly commit?
[05:59] Alex: predictable commit. our finance wants a baseline we can forecast for. but we also want clear overage/burst rules so we don't get surprises.
[06:09] Maya: we can provide committed reserved option with burst credits and a clear overage rate. we'll outline burst throttles and prewarm windows in the proposal.
[06:19] Jordan: encryption at rest and in transit — we need customer-managed keys for model artifacts and logs. do you support that?
[06:26] Connor: yes, KMS/HSM integrations are supported; we can store model artifacts encrypted and integrate with your key provider. note: some audit log retention options vary by plan.
[06:37] Priya: should we be worried about quality regressions when you apply batching and quantization? we run a lot of fine prompts that are sensitive.
[06:47] Connor: that's a great point — Redwood Optimize includes evaluation hooks so you can run prompt sets against each variant; we can attach regression alerts and rollback policies. for the POC we'll include evaluation on your prompt set.
[07:03] Alex: what about multi-region latency? some of our customers are EU-based and we need regional routing and data residency.
[07:12] Maya: we can pin models to regions and route by customer region. for data residency we have Private options (VPC/on-prem) where control plane is private. Dedicated can be provisioned in specific regions as well.
[07:26] Jordan: do you support SAML/SSO and RBAC for users? we need tight access controls for ops.
[07:32] Maya: yes SAML, Okta integrations, and RBAC are supported; we can share the security checklist.
[07:40] Priya: any reference benchmarks i can glance at? we want something close to our workload — chat heavy with short sequences.
[07:47] Connor: we'll share a benchmark spreadsheet and a perf deck; still the best is a POC with your prompts.
[07:54] Alex: timeline: we'd like a pilot before the end of month if possible.
[07:59] Maya: sounds doable — plan is: we send sizing/pricing + security docs by Friday, get your logs, then schedule the 1-day POC wk of Feb 23.
[08:11] Jordan: about monitoring and billing — can you show token-level cost breakdowns? we need per-tenant cost centers.
[08:20] Connor: yes console shows token-level cost and per-route dashboards; for Dedicated we'll also provide tenant-level breakdowns and exportable reports for chargeback.
[08:32] Priya: small nit — how do you measure a token? we have different tokenizers for some models.
[08:37] Connor: good call — we base on model tokenizer; in the POC we'll standardize on the tokenizer that matches your models and include conversion notes.
[08:47] Alex: any legal/procurement notes? we'll need typical s s p and data processing terms.
[08:53] Maya: procurement — we'll attach standard enterprise T C S and data processing addendum. if you have custom clauses we can route to legal after the POC.
[09:02] Priya: ok, sounds good. one more technical — autoscaling timelines, how fast can you spin new nodes answering short bursts?
[09:09] Connor: autoscale is policy-driven; cold spin to provision new host and load model can take 30-120s depending on model size unless you keep a warm buffer. we recommend a small warm buffer to cover short spikes.
[09:22] Alex: if we set warm buffer, is that billed as reserved capacity?
[09:27] Maya: yes the warm buffer is part of the reserved commitment; burst beyond that uses burst credits or overage rates, which we'll specify.
[09:36] Jordan: for the POC please include a network partition test and a heavy 4k sequence job to understand degraded behavior.
[09:44] Connor: noted, we'll include both scenarios plus evaluation metrics and traces.
[09:51] Maya: recap of next steps: we'll send pricing and security docs, connor will prepare POC plan, crestline will share logs and prompts, and we schedule the POC. any other items?
[10:03] Alex: that's it from me, thanks.
[10:06] Priya: thanks all.
[10:08] Maya: thanks everyone, i'll follow up via email with the links and actions.

End of transcript.
